chapters.title: Replication
chapters.hook: The store photo matched perfectly; the mystery-shop note said the service had not survived the copy.
chapters.counterintuition: Exact sameness can be the failed copy. Replication succeeds only when the working structure transfers with enough fidelity to persist.
chapters.tryThisNow: Choose one process you want repeated. Hand it to someone else, watch the first attempt, and revise the step where structure failed to transfer.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Replication preserves essential structure through transmission; copying the surface ritual is useless when the working pattern does not survive transfer.

breakdown.fastRead:
Teresa's training binder made the new store look identical. The store photo matched the original counter, menu board, and greeting card. Then the mystery-shop note said customers waited while staff copied the words without understanding the service rhythm.

She stopped fixing decoration and rewrote the transfer: when to greet, when to move, when to notice a line forming.

Replication is persistence through copying. The copy has to carry the working structure, not just the visible shell.
breakdown.deepRead:
"The checklist was on the tray," William said after the handoff review. The sterile checklist had been copied, laminated, and initialed. The new team still missed the timing because the initials grid did not show who owned each step.

The support stays focused: replication means copying, transmission, and persistence without needing technical biology. William's problem was not that the old team had failed to document. It was that the essential structure had not transferred. A good copy preserves what makes the pattern work after the original expert steps away. Fidelity is about function, not perfect resemblance. If the new team cannot run the handoff without the senior nurse whispering the real order, the copy has not carried the pattern.

A copy that cannot run is only evidence of copying.

Gabrielle saw the same error in tutoring. Students copied answers from a worked example and still failed the next problem. The reasoning notebook showed where replication broke: they had copied the result, not the question sequence. She recorded a student explaining each step, then revised the example so the method, not the answer, could travel.

The limit is overcontrol. Perfect sameness can block useful local adjustment. Replication should preserve the working structure while allowing the surface to fit the new setting.
breakdown.fullRead:
At 7:42 a.m., Stellan left a style sheet for the guest editor and expected the newsletter to sound right. The newsletter proof had the same section order, the same short headline style, and the same signoff. The guest draft still felt wrong because it copied the format without carrying the judgment behind the edits.

Replication extends a system beyond one current instance. A franchise store, a surgical checklist, a tutoring method, an editorial playbook, a glaze recipe, or a volunteer script all face the same test: can someone else reproduce the pattern when the original keeper is absent? If not, the system has not replicated. It has staged a resemblance.

What must survive for the copy to work?

That question changes documentation. You stop recording only the surface and start recording the structure: the sequence, constraint, feedback signal, exception, and reason for the move. Teresa needed service rhythm, not decor. William needed ownership timing, not laminated paper. Gabrielle needed reasoning steps, not answer shapes. Stellan needed editorial judgment, not a pretty style sheet.

A useful replication test has two parts. First, the second person must use the process without the original keeper standing nearby. Second, the result must show the same function under ordinary variation. A store can have different floor tile and still replicate service. A newsletter can use a different example and still replicate editorial judgment. A glaze can move through a different pair of hands and still produce the surface the studio promised.

You can feel the difference in a ceramics studio. Nathan gives a glaze card to an assistant, and the test tile comes out dull. The card lists ingredients, but the kiln shelf position changes the heat. "I followed the recipe," the assistant says. Nathan has to decide whether the recipe is complete or whether the working structure includes the shelf location, timing, and visible surface cue. The revised card does not tell the assistant to imitate Nathan's posture or favorite brush. It tells them which conditions make the glaze repeatable.

Eva found the same pattern with volunteer onboarding. A welcome script sounded friendly when she used it, but Saturday volunteers skipped the task card and left new people standing with name badges and no work. The script replicated tone. It did not replicate the onboarding structure. She revised the handoff so the next volunteer could welcome, assign, and check back without her. The second volunteer became the proof: if they could run the welcome table and the new person knew where to go, the structure had traveled.

Replication can spread bad structure too. A copied error becomes more dangerous as it travels. Before making a process easy to repeat, ask whether it deserves persistence. Transmission gives power to whatever pattern you preserve, including shortcuts, blind spots, and hidden dependencies.

Make the second person the test. If the copy fails, do not blame the person first. Look for the missing structure that only lived in the original operator's head.

examples.title: Teresa Watches the Second Store
examples.scenario: The training binder smells like fresh plastic when Teresa gives it to the second store manager before the lunch rush. She predicts the store photo will preserve the original service, down to the counter angle and greeting card. The mystery-shop note reveals the failure: the counter looks right, but staff do not know when to greet, move, or notice the line. Teresa must choose function over resemblance.
examples.whatToDo: Revise the binder around the service sequence and line cues, then test it with another manager before opening.
examples.whyItMatters: The copied decor did not replicate the working structure. Fidelity means the service pattern survives transfer.

examples.title: William Revises the Initials Grid
examples.scenario: "We used the checklist," William says during the postmortem, pointing at the sterile tray after a delayed room turnover. The handoff tray was prepared, and every copied line was initialed, but the initials grid never made ownership clear to the new team. He must decide now whether the copied document is enough or whether timing and responsibility need to be part of the replication.
examples.whatToDo: Add ownership and timing to the initials grid, then watch a new team run the handoff without the senior nurse prompting.
examples.whyItMatters: The checklist did not persist as a working pattern until the handoff structure traveled with it.

examples.title: Gabrielle Records the Reasoning
examples.scenario: The study room whiteboard still shows Gabrielle's worked example while a student's reasoning notebook sits blank beside a half-erased equation. The student copied every answer shape and failed the next problem when the numbers changed. Gabrielle faces a decision before the next session: provide more examples, or record the question sequence so the reasoning can replicate.
examples.whatToDo: Have the student explain each step into a recording and revise the worked example around prompts, not final answers.
examples.whyItMatters: Answer copying created surface repetition. The method persisted only when the reasoning structure transferred.

examples.title: Stellan Rewrites the Style Sheet
examples.scenario: At 7:42 a.m., Stellan opens the guest draft beside the style sheet and newsletter proof, with the send queue already scheduled. The sections match, but the judgment is off: weak claims stay, sharp details disappear, and the lead paragraph wanders. Before the next issue, Stellan has to decide whether to police wording or document the editing choices the guest editor must reproduce.
examples.whatToDo: Revise the playbook around judgment tests: what to cut, what to keep, and how each section earns space.
examples.whyItMatters: The layout copied easily. The editorial structure needed explicit transmission to persist without Stellan.

examples.title: Nathan Marks the Kiln Shelf
examples.scenario: You hold the glaze card while Nathan studies a dull test tile from the lower kiln shelf, still warm enough to smell faintly mineral. "I followed the recipe," the assistant says, pointing to each measured ingredient. Nathan hovers over two fixes: scold the measurement, or add shelf position, timing, and surface cues so the glaze can be replicated.
examples.whatToDo: Add kiln shelf position and visual cues to the glaze card, then test the recipe with a second assistant.
examples.whyItMatters: The ingredient list was only part of the structure. Replication failed where the recipe omitted conditions that shaped the result.

examples.title: Eva Tests the Welcome Script
examples.scenario: It took Eva three Saturdays to notice that new volunteers left with name badges but no assigned work after the morning rush. The welcome script sounded warm, yet the task card stayed on the table beside untouched gloves. She must choose between rewriting friendly lines or testing whether another volunteer can welcome, assign, and check back without her.
examples.whatToDo: Add the assignment step and check-back cue to the script, then watch a volunteer onboard the next person.
examples.whyItMatters: The tone replicated, but the onboarding structure did not. Persistence requires the working pattern to survive the handoff.

questions.prompt: A franchise store copies the original counter, menu board, greeting card, and store photo, but customers wait longer and service feels wrong during lunch. What should be replicated?
choices: The service rhythm and cues that make the format work.
Only the decor visible in photos.
A longer binder with more slogans.
questions.explanation: Replication needs the working structure. Surface resemblance is weak if the service sequence does not transfer.

questions.prompt: A surgical checklist is copied for a new team and placed on the sterile tray, but nobody knows who owns each step during the room handoff. Which fix fits replication?
choices: Laminate the same checklist again.
Add timing and responsibility to the initials grid and test it without prompting.
Tell the new team to copy the senior nurse's style.
questions.explanation: The missing structure is ownership during transfer. More copies of the same surface document will not preserve the handoff.

questions.prompt: Students copy answers from worked examples into a reasoning notebook, but cannot solve new problems when the numbers change. What should the tutor transmit?
choices: More answer shapes to memorize.
A nicer final answer template.
The reasoning prompts that generate the answer.
questions.explanation: The method is the essential structure. Copying results creates surface sameness without transferable reasoning.

questions.prompt: A guest editor follows the newsletter layout and headline format, but misses which claims to cut and which details to keep before send time. What is the replication problem?
choices: Guest editors should never be trusted.
The playbook copied format but failed to transmit editorial judgment.
The newsletter needs a different font.
questions.explanation: The format traveled; the working judgment did not. Replication requires the structure behind decisions.

questions.prompt: A ceramics assistant follows the ingredient card exactly, but the glaze changes because shelf position, timing, and surface cues were never documented. What should be revised?
choices: The assistant's attitude.
The recipe to include the conditions that shape the result.
The studio logo on the card.
questions.explanation: The ingredient list omitted essential conditions. Fidelity depends on transmitting what actually produces the glaze.

questions.prompt: A volunteer script sounds friendly at the welcome table, but new volunteers leave with badges and no tasks after the morning rush. What is the strongest diagnosis?
choices: Volunteers dislike friendly scripts.
Name badges are the only important part.
The tone replicated while the onboarding structure failed.
questions.explanation: The script transmitted surface tone but not assignment and check-back steps. The working pattern did not persist.

questions.prompt: A manager asks every branch to copy the flagship exactly, including decor and phrases, even though local constraints and customer flow differ. What should replication preserve?
choices: The essential structure that produces results, with surfaces adjusted to context.
Every decoration and phrase regardless of fit.
Only the parts easiest to photograph.
questions.explanation: Replication is not blind sameness. It preserves the working structure while allowing local surfaces to fit.

questions.prompt: A playbook lets a second team run the process successfully without the founder present, even though the room setup and staff mix differ. How should you evaluate it?
choices: It likely replicated the essential structure rather than just surface ritual.
It failed because the room was not identical.
It should remove all local judgment.
questions.explanation: Success without the founder suggests the structure persisted. Exact surface sameness is less important than transferred function.

questions.prompt: A sales team copies a top performer's email wording but not the qualification questions she asks before sending it, and results drop across new accounts. What response transfers the model?
choices: Copy the email font more closely.
Tell everyone to send more messages.
Document and practice the qualification sequence that makes the email work.
questions.explanation: The effective structure is the qualification sequence. The wording alone is a surface copy that cannot carry the method.

reviewCards.front: A copied process looks right and fails. What should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve replication: identify the working structure that failed to transfer, not the surface that copied well.

reviewCards.front: A copied checklist looks right but fails in a new team's hands. What should you retrieve about fidelity?
reviewCards.back: Fidelity means the function persists. The copy carries the sequence, constraints, and feedback that make the pattern work.

reviewCards.front: A process works only when the founder is nearby. What does a second-person test reveal?
reviewCards.back: A second person exposes what only lived in the original operator's head.

reviewCards.front: A branch copies every surface detail and still fails locally. When can exact sameness hurt replication?
reviewCards.back: When local conditions differ and rigid surfaces block the structure from working in the new setting.

reviewCards.front: A bad shortcut is about to become part of a playbook. What danger comes with making a process easy to copy?
reviewCards.back: Bad structure can spread too. Decide whether the pattern deserves persistence before transmitting it.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to preserve the working structure through transfer. The skill is testing whether another person can reproduce the function without copying only the surface.

ifThenPlans.plan: If I write a playbook, then I will include the sequence, constraint, feedback signal, and exception behind the visible steps.
If someone copies the answer but fails the next case, then I will teach the reasoning structure before adding more examples.
If a new team follows the form and still fails, then I will watch the handoff to find the missing structure.
If a second location opens, then I will test whether the core service pattern works before matching the decor.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Today, hand one repeatable process to someone else for a small test. Watch where the structure fails to transfer and revise that step.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, choose one process you rely on and ask what must survive for it to replicate without you.

A copy that cannot run is only evidence of copying.
Make the second person the test.

chapters.title: Cooperation
chapters.hook: The cleaning log explained why the lab calendar looked full while the machine sat idle.
chapters.counterintuition: Friendly people can still produce selfish systems. Cooperation works when the shared design makes contribution easier than taking the benefit and leaving the cost.
chapters.tryThisNow: For one shared task, make each contribution visible. Add a rule for the handoff, then remove one easy way to benefit without helping.
chapters.keyTakeaway: Cooperation requires coordination rules, visible contributions, and aligned costs so joint outcomes beat private shortcuts.

breakdown.fastRead:
Alice found the equipment calendar packed with reservations and the machine idle under a dusty cover. The reservation tag showed who booked it. The cleaning log showed who left it unusable.

After the postmortem, she changed the rule: no new reservation until the previous user signed the cleaning line and released the tag.

Cooperation is coordinated action among multiple actors. Good feeling helps, but shared outcomes need rules that make contribution visible and defection costly.
breakdown.deepRead:
"I can cover pickup today, but I cannot be the backup every week," Robert said while the pickup board hung beside the snack sign-up. Parents liked the childcare co-op. The spare key kept landing with the same two people.

The frame is simple: cooperation involves coordination, shared cost, mutual benefit, alignment, and joint outcome. Robert did not need everyone to become more agreeable. He needed a rule that matched benefits to contribution. The pickup board, snack sign-up, and spare key had to show who carried the shared work and who quietly leaned on others. Cooperation needs a visible ledger.

Agreeable people can still defect quietly.

Henri saw the same pattern in a product launch. The dependency map looked collaborative until the launch checklist exposed unowned tasks. Every team said it was aligned. The owner tags told the truth. Work that belongs to everyone can become work owned by no one, so Henri changed the coordination rule before the launch date turned into blame.

The limit is over-policing. Cooperation dies if every action becomes surveillance. The goal is enough visibility and alignment to make mutual gain easier, not a culture of suspicion. Track the contribution that protects the joint outcome, then stop. A board that clarifies the handoff helps; a board that turns every parent or teammate into a suspect destroys the trust it meant to preserve.
breakdown.fullRead:
At 5:40 a.m., Vera checked the radio channel card while rain hit the rescue truck roof. The grid map showed search zones with patchy coverage, and the battery meter on one team's radio was already low. Everyone wanted the missing hiker found. Wanting the same outcome did not make the search coordinated.

Cooperation becomes real through coordination cost. The cost is not only effort; it is timing, attention, restraint, and a willingness to make your part legible to others. Someone must use the shared channel. Someone must report grid status. Someone must preserve battery. Someone must avoid clogging the air with duplicate updates. Without those rules, each team can work hard and still make the joint outcome worse.

Where can a person benefit from the group while skipping the shared cost?

That question is uncomfortable, which is why people avoid it. They prefer to call cooperation a mood: be nice, be aligned, be team-oriented. The practical model is harder and more useful. It asks how contribution is made visible, how handoffs are timed, how shared costs are distributed, and how quiet defection is prevented before resentment takes over.

You can see the same structure backstage at a theater. Peter studies the paint schedule while the lumber list sits half finished. The set builders are friendly, but crews collide because everyone saves their preferred work for later. A crew badge without a visible contribution rule becomes decoration. Peter has to decide whether to keep asking for goodwill or change the schedule so painting, cutting, and assembly stop blocking each other.

Ignacio learned it at the farmers market. The stall lottery slip was meant to keep busy-season locations fair, but the cash box and market map showed a pattern: a few vendors arrived late, kept strong spots, and skipped cleanup. In the postmortem, he did not lecture vendors about community. He changed the rotation rule so stall priority depended on cleanup and cash-box closing duties, not only luck.

Cooperation has an ethical edge. A group can coordinate around a bad outcome, and efficient alignment can make harm travel faster. Mutual gain for insiders may create costs for outsiders. The model clarifies coordination; judgment still has to ask who benefits and who pays. A cartel can cooperate. A rumor chain can cooperate. A team can coordinate around hiding a defect. The word cooperation sounds warm, but the mechanism is neutral until you inspect the outcome it serves.

Design cooperation as a path, not a wish. Make the shared outcome specific. Make contribution visible. Make the handoff clear. Then make the quiet shortcut less attractive than doing the part that keeps the joint outcome alive.

examples.title: Alice Signs the Cleaning Line
examples.scenario: The equipment calendar is full, the reservation tag is clipped to a silent machine, and the cleaning log has three blank lines from the previous week. In the postmortem, Alice sees that everyone booked shared time while cleanup fell to whoever arrived next and lost the first twenty minutes. She must choose between another polite reminder and a rule tying reservations to signed cleanup.
examples.whatToDo: Require the previous user to sign the cleaning log before the next reservation opens. Make contribution visible at the handoff.
examples.whyItMatters: Cooperation failed because benefits were private and costs were hidden. The new rule makes shared use easier than quiet defection.

examples.title: Robert Moves the Spare Key
examples.scenario: "I can cover today," Robert says, but the pickup board shows his name in four boxes and his spare key has become the unofficial backup plan. The snack sign-up is full of initials from parents who never take emergency pickup. Before next week, Robert has to decide whether to keep absorbing the gap or rotate pickups and snacks together.
examples.whatToDo: Pair pickup turns with snack sign-up and rotate the spare key visibly. Make every family carry a fair part of the shared cost.
examples.whyItMatters: The co-op depends on mutual benefit. A few parents cannot preserve cooperation while others benefit quietly.

examples.title: Henri Adds Owner Tags
examples.scenario: The dependency map stretches across the war-room wall while the launch checklist keeps one blank owner tag beside the API handoff. Every team says it is aligned, the status slide is green, and nobody can say who will test the final connection. Henri faces the choice before the release meeting: accept shared language, or force visible ownership for each blocking dependency.
examples.whatToDo: Add owner tags to every launch dependency and require handoff confirmation before the checklist can close.
examples.whyItMatters: Alignment talk did not coordinate the work. Cooperation improved when the joint outcome had visible owners.

examples.title: Vera Protects the Channel
examples.scenario: At 5:40 a.m., Vera taps the radio channel card as rain hits the truck roof and static fills the speaker. "Use channel two only for grid updates," she says, watching a battery meter flash low while two teams talk over each other. Teams want to help, but she must decide whether to allow free-form radio chatter or enforce the protocol that keeps the grid map usable.
examples.whatToDo: Set the radio rule, require grid-status updates, and preserve battery by limiting nonessential chatter.
examples.whyItMatters: Shared intent is not enough in a storm. Cooperation depends on coordination rules that protect the joint search.

examples.title: Peter Reorders the Paint Schedule
examples.scenario: You see Peter's paint schedule taped beside a lumber list with missing cuts and two crews waiting at the same stage door. Crew badges hang neatly, but painters and builders keep blocking each other because no handoff proves the previous step is finished. Peter hovers over two paths: ask everyone to be nicer, or sequence paint, lumber, and assembly so each crew's contribution is visible before the next begins.
examples.whatToDo: Reorder the schedule around handoffs and mark each crew's completed contribution before the next crew starts.
examples.whyItMatters: Friendliness did not remove collisions. Cooperation needed a coordination rule that made joint progress easier.

examples.title: Ignacio Rewrites the Lottery
examples.scenario: It took Ignacio half a season to see the stall lottery slip was not creating fairness. The market map revealed the same vendors near the entrance, the cash box closed late when cleanup was skipped, and newer vendors began arriving discouraged. He has to choose between defending the old lottery or tying prime spots to visible shared duties.
examples.whatToDo: Link stall rotation to cleanup and cash-box closing duties, then publish the market map before each week starts.
examples.whyItMatters: A fair-sounding lottery allowed quiet defection. Cooperation improved when benefits and shared costs were coordinated.

questions.prompt: A lab calendar is full, but the shared machine sits dirty because cleanup is invisible and the next team loses twenty minutes before every reservation. Which cooperation move should come first?
choices: Tie new reservations to a signed cleaning log.
Ask everyone to be more considerate in general.
Buy a second machine before changing behavior.
questions.explanation: The rule makes contribution visible and blocks quiet defection. General niceness leaves the shared cost hidden.

questions.prompt: A childcare co-op has a pickup board, snack sign-up, and spare key, but the same parents cover every emergency while others keep the benefits. What should change?
choices: Let reliable parents keep absorbing gaps.
Pair pickup turns and snack sign-ups so each family carries visible shared cost.
Cancel the board and rely on group messages.
questions.explanation: Cooperation needs aligned contribution. Pairing duties makes mutual benefit easier and prevents quiet dependence on a few parents.

questions.prompt: A launch team says it is aligned, but the dependency map has blank owner tags for blocking tasks and nobody can name the API handoff owner. What is the best cooperation fix?
choices: Hold a morale session about teamwork.
Wait until launch day exposes the gaps.
Assign visible owners and handoff confirmations for every dependency.
questions.explanation: Alignment language is weak without coordination. Owner tags make contribution and responsibility visible.

questions.prompt: Search teams share the same goal, but radio chatter drains batteries, blocks grid updates, and turns the storm search into duplicate work. Which action fits the model?
choices: Set a radio protocol that reserves the channel for grid status and battery-critical updates.
Let every team speak whenever it wants because intention is good.
Stop using the grid map.
questions.explanation: The protocol coordinates shared action under cost. Good intent can still damage the joint outcome when channels are scarce.

questions.prompt: A theater build has friendly crews, but painters and carpenters block the same stage door because lumber and paint schedules never confirm handoffs. What should the director diagnose?
choices: The crews need better personalities.
The handoff rule is missing, so cooperation depends on goodwill alone.
The show should cut every set piece.
questions.explanation: The conflict is coordination, not attitude. Sequenced handoffs make joint work easier than collision.

questions.prompt: A market stall lottery sounds fair, but vendors who skip cleanup still get prime locations and the cash box closes late. What is the strongest response?
choices: Assume vendors will feel guilty eventually.
Tie stall rotation to visible cleanup and cash-box duties.
Give permanent prime spots to the loudest vendors.
questions.explanation: The old rule allowed benefit without contribution. Cooperation improves when shared costs affect access to shared benefits.

questions.prompt: A manager equates cooperation with avoiding conflict, so nobody raises dependency failures until deadlines slip and the shared launch date collapses. What is wrong?
choices: Cooperation requires constant argument.
Conflict avoidance can hide the coordination failures cooperation must solve.
Deadlines should be removed so conflict disappears.
questions.explanation: Cooperation is coordinated action, not pleasant silence. Surfacing dependency failures protects the joint outcome.

questions.prompt: A neighborhood tool shed works because checkout, maintenance, broken-part replacement, and member costs are visible at the moment people borrow tools. How should you evaluate it?
choices: It is too structured to count as cooperation.
It should hide costs to preserve friendliness.
It likely coordinates mutual benefit by making contribution and shared costs visible.
questions.explanation: Visible cost and contribution support cooperation. Structure can make mutual gain easier than private shortcuts.

questions.prompt: A shared software library is useful, but teams skip documentation and leave others to debug changes after each merge. Which response transfers the model?
choices: Praise collaboration in the next meeting.
Ban shared libraries entirely.
Require docs and owner tags before a shared change can merge.
questions.explanation: The merge rule links shared benefit to visible contribution. It reduces quiet defection by making the handoff explicit.

reviewCards.front: A group wants the same outcome but keeps colliding. What should you retrieve?
reviewCards.back: Retrieve cooperation as coordination: make handoffs, contribution, and shared costs visible.

reviewCards.front: Why is agreeableness not enough for cooperation?
reviewCards.back: People can be pleasant while costs stay hidden and responsibilities remain unowned.

reviewCards.front: What does quiet defection look like?
reviewCards.back: Someone benefits from the shared system while skipping the contribution that keeps it working.

reviewCards.front: How do you avoid turning cooperation into surveillance?
reviewCards.back: Make only the necessary contributions and handoffs visible enough to support mutual gain.

reviewCards.front: What ethical question should follow efficient cooperation?
reviewCards.back: Ask who benefits and who pays, because groups can coordinate around harmful outcomes too.

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to make mutual gain easier than quiet defection. The skill is designing coordination rules that expose contribution and protect shared outcomes.

ifThenPlans.plan: If people use a shared resource, then I will connect access to the visible contribution that keeps it usable.
If everyone says they are aligned, then I will check for owner tags and handoff confirmations.
If a few people carry the recurring work, then I will make the shared cost visible and rotate it with the shared benefit.
If multiple teams share scarce channels or tools, then I will set a coordination rule before action fragments.

implementationPlan.twentyFourHourChallenge: Today, find one shared task where contribution is hidden. Add one visible handoff or owner rule that makes mutual gain easier.
implementationPlan.weeklyPractice: Each week, review one cooperative system for quiet defection: who benefits, who contributes, and where the rule needs alignment.
